implementation_notes: Python raises freely, and the common validation libraries signal by exception or return early, so the pattern-faithful form is a small @dataclass with an errors list plus add/has_errors, returned by the validation function; field(default_factory=list) gives each call its own list. Choose the pydantic variant when declarative parsing and coercion matter more than the return-based contract; Django forms sit in between, since form.is_valid() returns a boolean while form.errors carries every field error.
pitfalls: A class-level mutable default (errors: list = []) is shared by every instance and leaks errors across requests; use field(default_factory=list).
A check that raises (or calls int()/datetime.strptime unguarded) aborts the whole pass and defeats the accumulation.
dataclasses.asdict() deep-copies every entry; on hot paths pass the list itself or make the entries frozen.

variants.name: pydantic model validation
variants.implementation_notes: pydantic validates the whole model before reporting: model_validate raises a single ValidationError whose .errors() returns one dict per failure (loc, type, msg, input), so the caller still sees every problem in one pass - but it signals by exception, which is precisely what Fowler argues against for expected failures. Use it for parsing and coercion at the boundary and convert the error list into the notification the API layer returns.
pitfalls: model_validate_json raises the same ValidationError, so the try/except is the interface - there is no non-throwing result to inspect.
exc.errors() includes the rejected input by default and can echo sensitive values into logs or responses; hide or filter it before serialising.
Nested models nest the failures: loc paths such as ('items', 3, 'sku') must be preserved, not flattened to their last element.
